result.reason: All four items form a single continuous exchange: Rava's *kan nimtze'u kan hayu* principle (item 1), Abaye's objection about the intermediate post-*kiddushin* period (item 2), Rava's response about *ein adam shoteh be'kos* (item 3), and the Gemara's follow-up challenge about *ein adam mitpayes be'mumim* (item 4) — exactly the content described in candidate 2 ('Abaye's Question') prose.

Both items together present the core argument about two presumptions (chazakat ha'guf + ein adam shoteh be'kos) operating in her favor when blemishes are post-kiddushin, versus only one presumption available pre-kiddushin, which is precisely what the 'Two Presumptions' prose section describes.

The passage presents Rav Ashi's explanation distinguishing 'mana l'abba biyadeich' (father's house/father's claim) from 'mana li biyadeich' (husband's house/woman's own claim), which is precisely what the 'Father's Claim' section's prose describes.

Both items together form the baraita challenge and its resolution (yateret answer), which is precisely what candidate 1 'Braita Challenge' describes — Rav Acha's objection to Rav Ashi and the question of why the father bears the burden for congenital blemishes.

The passage contains Shmuel's donkey-and-cow case plus the Gemara's attempt to identify which part of the kallah mishnah provides the parallel—the bride in father's house vs. father-in-law's house comparison—which is precisely what candidate 2 ('Comparison') describes in its prose.

The passage — Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak identifying the proof as coming from the bride-in-father's-house case specifically with regard to betrothal/kiddushin money — directly introduces the analysis elaborated in the 'Burden Analysis' prose, which explains why the kallah's possession of the ring is conditional and how that parallels the donkey-owner's burden.

The passage directly discusses whether kiddushin money given le'tivu'a must be returned in a case of kiddushei ta'ut, which matches exactly the 'Ring Conditional' prose about the le'tivu'a dispute and its application to mistaken betrothal.
The passage is the Gemara's introduction of the needle-in-stomach baraita, which is exactly what the 'Needle Case' section's prose describes and analyzes.
